21 The graph shows the extension of a sample of a type of rubber as different loads F are applied
and then gradually removed.

What is the best estimate of the strain energy in the rubber when a load of 80 N is applied?
A
0.40 J
B
0.64 J
C
0.88 J
D
1.3 J

hints: Look at the axes: vertical $F/\text{N}$ against horizontal extension/$\text{mm}$. Find the extension where the loading curve reaches $F = 80\text{ N}$, about $16\text{ mm}$.
Recall strain energy is the area under the loading $F$ against $x$ curve, and this rubber graph is curved so $0.5Fx$ for a straight line does not apply.

Compare with the triangle $0.5 \times 80\text{ N} \times 0.016\text{ m}$. Notice the curve at $4\text{ mm}$ is already at $40\text{ N}$, well above the straight line, so the true area must be clearly larger than $0.64\text{ J}$.
walkthrough: Read the graph at $F = 80\text{ N}$. The curve reaches $80\text{ N}$ at extension $x \approx 16\text{ mm} = 0.016\text{ m}$.
State the rule: strain energy stored on loading $= $ area under the $F$ against $x$ loading curve from $0$ to $x$, i.e. $E = \int F\,dx$.
Check linearity: the graph curves steeply at first then flattens, so rubber does not obey Hooke's law and $E \ne 0.5Fx$.

Estimate the area. The triangle to $(0.016\text{ m}, 80\text{ N})$ is $0.5 \times 80 \times 0.016 = 0.64\text{ J}$. The actual curve lies above this line, for example $F \approx 40\text{ N}$ at only $4\text{ mm}$.

Count grid squares under the curve up to $16\text{ mm}$. Each large $20\text{ N}$ by $4\text{ mm}$ square is $20 \times 0.004 = 0.08\text{ J}$. About 11 such squares lie under the curve, giving $11 \times 0.08 \approx 0.88\text{ J}$.
This area is the best estimate of stored strain energy. This is option C.

A.explanation: Too small. It underestimates the area under the $F$ against extension curve up to $80\text{ N}$.

B.explanation: This is $0.5 \times 80 \times 0.016 = 0.64\text{ J}$, the triangle area. It applies only if Hooke's law were obeyed, but the rubber curve lies above the straight line.

C.explanation: The area under the loading curve to extension about $16\text{ mm}$ at $80\text{ N}$ is about $0.88\text{ J}$ by square counting.

D.explanation: Too large. It is close to the rectangle $80 \times 0.016 = 1.28\text{ J}$ and ignores the curved shape below that rectangle.
